FAST

Nov 10 : Anthropic's IPO plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion, a regulatory filing showed on Tuesday, testing Wall Street's faith in the AI boom amid growing worries about its risks. The company is targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion, according to Reuters calculations based on the outstanding shares listed in the filing. Reuters exclusively reported on Tuesday that Anthropic and some of its investors aim to sell shares in an indicative price band of between $70 and $78 per share. The company is launching the roadshow for a historic share sale that is expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fueled a massive influx of capital into AI companies.

COMMENTS: FIONA CINCOTTA, SENIOR MARKET ANALYST, CITY INDEX, LONDON "It's a little bit lower than an initial expectation around the 69 billion that was sent out earlier this morning, but that was then considered inaccurate. And I think given the volatility, concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week. This is actually fairly bullish and it's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there." IPEK OZKARDESKAYA, SENIOR ANALYST AT SWISSQUOTE BANK, GENEVA, SWITZERLAND "What we are seeing is essentially a reassessment of Anthropic's value in a more challenging AI environment. The company continues to post impressive growth, but investors are increasingly focused on the cost of generating that growth. The shift from a $2 trillion valuation to today's level reflects a change in focus from revenue growth alone to the significant financial commitments and spending required to sustain it." "The timing of the IPO is notable because investors have become much more focused on the costs of the AI buildout than they were over the past few years. Political and regulatory uncertainties, along with a higher interest-rate environment, have also raised questions about future AI spending. As a result, many investors see Anthropic's IPO as an important test of appetite for AI-related investments." MICHAEL BAKER, HEAD OF UK PREMIUM CLIENTS AT CAPITAL.COM, LONDON "You've got to build a sustainable client base that is willing to pay those sizeable bills, both on the consumer side and among businesses, that's what Anthropic will have to sustain. At the same time, it has to keep up with the costs of chips and data centers while continuing to offer competitive models and outperform major Chinese rivals." "It's a huge valuation, and I think it will take a lot to convince investors that it represents a fair price."

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : Bond investors are growing more cautious on debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, highlighting concerns over the expected efforts of a Democrat-controlled Congress to slow the pace of AI investment and data center expansion. US high-yield credit spreads widened to 348 basis points in last Thursday's stock-market swoon, ICE BofA US Corporate Index data showed. That was the highest since May 2025, just a month after President Trump imposed global tariffs. Spreads narrowed on Friday to 342 basis points. "The markets are definitely anxious right now. I wouldn't be surprised to see some continued volatility in both high yield and loans," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York. While healthy corporate fundamentals continue to support the market, a deeper reassessment of AI-related risk could push credit spreads wider in both high-yield and investment-grade debt in anticipation of stricter regulations on this technology, analysts and portfolio managers said. Investment-grade spreads were at 93 basis points last Thursday, against 91 the previous session.

Democrats are already planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting AI systems and data center development when they take control of Congress in January. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology, but over the weekend, following a historic midterm loss for his party, he signaled openness to safeguards. "Appetite is more cautious and more discriminating," said Ali Hassan, portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management. "Political and regulatory scrutiny is prompting a review of credits up and down the chain, from developers to contractors to suppliers." MORE CAUTIOUS APPETITE Data center bonds, many of them concentrated in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, have come under fresh pressure in recent weeks, especially during the technology selloff. Single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, leading the deterioration in the high-yield market, analysts said, and hitting their highest levels since March. Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds fell to 89.25 cents on the dollar on November 5, for instance, lifting yields to 13 per cent from the 9.875 per cent offered when Galaxy Digital's wholly owned unit sold the B+ rated debt in late July. "A slowdown in the AI buildout that hits the supply chain, power producers, electrical contractors, equipment and machinery, data center developers, all of these are going to have a second-order effect," said Peter Yanulis, multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles. For investors, the larger concern is the potential impact of AI regulation on economic growth. Investment in artificial intelligence and the infrastructure underpinning it has been a major engine of US expansion, helping keep growth resilient this year despite broad uncertainties. "Any slowdown in the pace of data center development has the potential to materially slow overall business investment," said Abiel Reinhart, senior economist at J.P. Morgan. RELIEF FROM SUPPLY In the near term, some investors believe a slowdown is probably a healthy thing for the credit market and for AI companies themselves, as stricter AI regulations mean less bond issuance - which should help support prices. "We can expect a bit more relief from the open floodgates that we've experienced on the AI supply and the market can now digest this transition period over the next six to 12 months," said Loomis Sayles' Yanulis. While investors are reassessing longer-term growth expectations, they see little risk of an immediate pullback in borrowing or capital spending tied to projects already under construction. "The political and regulatory uncertainty could impact the later years, 2028-2030 (and later), but it is unlikely to significantly change the capex and issuance numbers for 2027 as many of those projects are already underway and capital commitments have been made," said Karen Choi, portfolio manager at Capital Group. While investors see little risk to near-term spending plans, many argue the bigger question is whether policy changes can meaningfully alter AI's long-term outlook. "AI is not going to slow down," said Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors. "If it's going to slow down in Texas, it will pop up somewhere in another state and just continue."

Source: Reuters

FAST

Nov 10 : Tesla’s move to discontinue its Cybertruck next year is perhaps the highest-profile flameout in a category that automakers had once hyped: huge electric pickups. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in a social media post on Saturday that the automaker would ramp up Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas, factory to meet an "order backlog” before dismantling the assembly line around June or July. He said the wind-down would allow Tesla to produce more Cybercab robotaxis, which have yet to be sold commercially. But sales of Tesla’s stainless-steel, angular truck — once described by MotorTrend magazine as having a “stealth-bomber-refrigerator design theme” — sagged 28 per cent this year through September, to about 11,600 trucks, according to an estimate from research firm Motor Intelligence. That sales pace is far off the 250,000-truck annual level Musk once predicted. Musk's other big company, SpaceX, also bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla at list price last year, according to a federal regulatory filing.

MORE MONEY FOR LESS TRUCK The market for large electric pickups has been a rough road for Tesla’s competitors, too. Even the Cybertruck’s relatively meager deliveries have outpaced sales of electric trucks from rivals General Motors and Ford Motor, where executives once had high hopes that battery-powered versions of their full-size pickups — their biggest moneymakers — would be major hits. Detroit’s automakers pivoted to EV pickup trucks early this decade in part to fend off entries from Tesla and Rivian. GM, Ford and Ram maker Stellantis for decades have cultivated legions of loyal truck customers by offering pickups with ever-increasing levels of horsepower and towing capability. But the companies have not been able to translate that formula to EV trucks, said Karl Brauer, executive analyst at vehicle research site iSeeCars.com. For one, the trucks are pricey, in part because their massive batteries are extremely costly. GM’s Chevrolet Silverado EV, for example, starts at around $62,000. Second, the trucks often struggle to perform tasks that owners of internal-combustion pickups have come to expect, like towing a horse trailer or hauling heavy equipment. “So in the end, you have to pay more money for a vehicle that is less functional,” Brauer said. AUTOMAKERS GO SMALLER, ADD GAS TO EXTEND RANGE Ford CEO Jim Farley acknowledged those tough economics during an earnings call last year, explaining why the company would discontinue the Ford Lightning, the electric version of its popular F-150 pickup that had been a relative hit for a few years before demand cooled. “The larger the vehicle, the bigger the battery, the more pressure on margin because customers will not pay a premium,” Farley said. Ford’s focus is now on a smaller electric pickup, the Fathom, which it plans to roll out late next year at a starting price of about $28,000. Automakers also are looking toward hybrid technology to deliver truck customers the functionality they need in an electric form. Stellantis next year plans to launch an extended-range electric pickup truck, which will use a gas-powered generator to recharge the battery on the go.

Source: Reuters

Nov 10 : Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is set to give the company a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly lower than some investors' expectations amid a recent cooling in investor appetite for AI, setting up a defining test of Wall Street's faith in the boom that it helped ignite. The company is launching the roadshow for a historic share sale that is expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fueled a massive influx of capital into AI companies. "What we are seeing is essentially a reassessment of Anthropic's value in a more challenging AI environment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank in Geneva. "The company continues to post impressive growth, but investors are increasingly focused on the cost of generating that growth." The AI lab and some of its investors are aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares in the IPO priced up to $78 per share.

Anthropic will also raise $26 billion via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors such as Alphabet's Google, Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices. Nvidia joined the deal amid an FBI probe into its CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese woman alleged to be a spy for Beijing, which has also triggered an internal investigation. Its filing spoke of a vision to "bring forth an age of miracles," even as it warned of existential risks to humanity, laying bare the extraordinary promise and profound uncertainties at the heart of the AI boom. The $1.4 trillion valuation target is on a fully diluted basis, which includes securities such as options and restricted stock. At the top of the marketed range, Anthropic would have a market value of about $1 trillion on a non-diluted basis. Investors had previously discussed a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, but expectations have since come down given the company's substantial infrastructure commitments and the recent volatility in AI-related stocks, with the $1.5 trillion figure viewed as the high end of the range, Reuters previously reported. "The shift from a $2 trillion valuation to today's level reflects a change in focus from revenue growth alone to the significant financial commitments and spending required to sustain it," Ozkardeskaya said. The second half of the year has brought a reckoning for the AI boom, as investors question whether returns will justify the massive spending and mounting debt costs in an elevated interest-rate environment. Concerns are also rising over the sustainability of the investment cycle, with questions around circular financing arrangements, the risk of infrastructure overcapacity and how quickly companies can turn their AI investments into revenue. The Nasdaq notched its deepest one-day drop in 19 months on Thursday, wiping out trillions in market value on fears of more AI scrutiny, particularly on data center construction, after Democrats' massive gains in the US midterm elections. Despite the midterms being widely viewed as a rebuff to a White House which has aggressively supported the AI build-out and opposed regulations, Anthropic adopted President Donald Trump's preferred name for the new technology, "Super Intelligence", at several points in its IPO filing. The prospectus outlined a range of risks facing both the company and the technology, warning that competitors could gain an edge by developing models faster and that advances in AI could outpace Anthropic's ability to put adequate safety and security measures in place. "Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," Anthropic warned in its latest prospectus. The warnings come amid a growing number of incidents involving "rogue" AI agents that have escaped sandboxed environments and breached private company systems, alongside concerns that increasingly capable AI tools could be used by hackers to penetrate protected networks. GROWTH COMES WITH RISKS Greater oversight and potential regulatory hurdles could complicate the infrastructure buildout underpinning the AI boom. But Anthropic's growth has so far defied those concerns, propelled by surging demand for its products, particularly its viral Claude models. Anthropic's run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30, according to the IPO filing. Anthropic's net loss narrowed in the third quarter as revenue jumped 47 per cent from a quarter earlier to $16.96 billion, though the pace of growth slowed. It had surged 144 per cent in the prior quarter. The company attributed the breakneck growth to the rapid adoption of Claude, including specialized products targeting industries such as healthcare, financial services and legal services. Anthropic's ambitions also come with enormous infrastructure costs. The company has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, highlighting how its rapid growth depends on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control. The listing move follows Elon Musk's SpaceX raising $75 billion in the world's largest IPO in June, at a valuation of nearly $1.75 trillion, excluding additional shares purchased by underwriters through the greenshoe option. Together with investments from cornerstones, which include Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft and TSMC, the Anthropic share offering will raise a total of up to $90.4 billion. Certain Anthropic board members and entities affiliated or associated with them have indicated interest in buying up to $303 million of shares from the offering. Anthropic, locked in a fierce battle for market share with rival OpenAI, was last valued at $965 billion in a private funding round. The company's prominent investors include Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital. Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, was founded in 2021 by a group of researchers who left OpenAI following disagreements over governance and AI safety. The shares are expected to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" after the IPO closes, which would make Anthropic one of the few major companies to go public this fall as higher borrowing costs, geopolitical turmoil and rising bond yields weigh on the IPO market. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the syndicate of investment banks underwriting the offering. Hours before Anthropic filed an updated prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday, details of its IPO, including the proposed price range, were briefly circulated to investment banks late on Monday shortly before being retracted, according to emails seen by Reuters. The preliminary terms showed Anthropic planned to sell about 867 million shares at $70 to $80 apiece, in an offering that could raise as much as $69.3 billion, including shares sold by existing shareholders. The prospectus ultimately filed with the SEC contained different terms, with Anthropic setting a lower price range and targeting proceeds of up to $64.4 billion.

Source: Reuters

FAST

Nov 10 : World stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook. Brent crude futures fell over 1.5 per cent, briefly dipping below the $90-a-barrel mark for the first time since late August, as investors pinned their hopes on possible peace talks between the US and Iran. The pan-European STOXX 600 index climbed 0.9 per cent, coming within 1 per cent of its all-time high as lower oil prices helped ease some inflation concerns which have been on investors' radar since the US-Israeli war with Iran erupted at the end of February. "The situation for Trump has changed politically with the midterms ... that probably makes it more likely that he wants to come to an accord with Iran before he's held back by Congress," said Joost van Leenders, senior investment strategist at Van Lanschot Kempen Investment Management in Amsterdam.

The stock rebound follows last week's rout in the wake of a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections that fed concerns new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade. Futures tracking the S&P 500 inched 0.1 per cent higher after the cash index clocked its biggest one-day jump since April on Monday and the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed 2.7 per cent higher, its best day in over three months. South Korea's KOSPI rose 4.4 per cent, while Japan's Nikkei gained 2.9 per cent. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares pushed 2 per cent higher, moving away from the seven-month low it hit last week. Earnings reports due this week from tech companies including CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the AI buildout and its profitability.  The next test of the AI trade would be Anthropic's public offering, with a regulatory filing showing the IPO is set to raise as much as $64.4 billion. The landmark listing will offer the first public-market assessment of the valuations, growth prospects and risks of frontier AI companies. NVIDIA STILL IN FOCUS       Market focus remains on Nvidia after Trump said on Monday that the FBI was looking into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. The company had said over the weekend that its board was probing whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation. A separate media report on Tuesday stated that Huang's affair facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of the company's chips. Nvidia shares edged 0.5 per cent higher in premarket trading after dropping 4.3 per cent on Monday. The company is also due to report earnings next week. Meanwhile, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank ought to raise short-term borrowing costs next month even if government data shows inflation cooled last month and should consider an upsized half-point rate hike if the inflation picture worsens. Data due at 8:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) is expected to show US consumer prices likely increased at a moderate pace in October, but inflation probably remained stubbornly high. "The latest remarks from Fed officials reinforced the case for additional hikes, even as financial-market volatility and uncertainty around AI-related investment supported a deliberate approach towards further tightening," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note. Traders are now almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December versus a 74 per cent chance seen a week earlier, the CME FedWatch tool showed after a blowout October jobs report on Friday. The 2-year Treasury note yield, which typically moves in step with Fed interest rate expectations, rose 6.5 basis points to 4.611 per cent. The US dollar held steady against both the Japanese yen and the euro.

Source: Reuters

Nov 10 : Honda is recalling 635,808 vehicles in the US over issues with the power steering assist software, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Tuesday. Here are some more details: • The recall involves certain 2021-2025 Acura TLX, 2022-2024 Acura MDX and 2023-2025 Pilot vehicles, the auto safety regulator said • NHTSA said that due to issues with the electronic power steering software, the system could enter a failsafe mode that disables the power steering assist and makes the vehicle harder to steer, increasing the risk of a crash • Dealers will reprogram the electronic power steering control unit, free of charge, as part of the recall remedy, NHTSA added

MUNICH, Nov 10 : German chipmaker Infineon needs commitments from customers to justify further expansion of its semiconductor production capacity, CEO Jochen Hanebeck said on Monday. Speaking at an industry event ahead of the electronica trade fair in Munich, Hanebeck said chipmakers were already investing heavily in production and research, but could not shoulder the financial risks of expansion alone. "There are limits to what we can shoulder," Hanebeck said, adding that customer commitments were "definitely" needed to bring additional capacity online. Infineon opened a new €5 billion ($5.6 billion) semiconductor factory in Dresden, Germany in July, and in October announced plans to invest around €1.1 billion in gallium nitride chip production in Villach, Austria.

SINGAPORE: Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed faces renewed scrutiny as the United States looks into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , alleged to be a spy for Beijing . Here are details of Megaspeed, where Huang used to be an executive. WHAT IS MEGASPEED? Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023, its business filings showed. It is wholly owned by Singapore-registered Swiftdata incorporated in October 2023, which says providing hosting services by non-data centres is its principal activity.

Two Singapore citizens are listed as officers of both companies. Tan Yong Pong was appointed a director of Swiftdata on Oct 31, 2023, before becoming a director of Megaspeed less than two weeks later. The same month, Huang Le ended an eight-month tenure as managing director of Megaspeed, media said. Huang Le is Alice Huang's Chinese name. Swiftdata also shares an address with Ng Wei Shi Khloe, who is listed as company secretary of both companies. Tan and Ng are the only listed officers of the two firms in their business filings. Reuters could not immediately contact Swiftdata, and Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia's advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted. On its website, it says it is an Nvidia Cloud Partner in the Asia-Pacific region and offers access to the company's GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 systems. Megaspeed's assets increased sharply to US$3 billion in 2024 from US$33 million in 2023, its business filings showed. It reported after-tax loss of US$20 million in 2024, versus a loss of US$21,283 a year earlier, while revenue jumped to US$294 million from zero. Its cashflow statement showed US$844,555 went to investing activities in 2024, after financing activities brought in cash of US$10 million the previous year.

Related:

From affair allegations to Nvidia probe: How the Jensen Huang controversy unfolded

Who is Alice Huang, Chinese exec accused of spying on Nvidia CEO?

SINGAPORE'S ROLE Last October Singapore police said they were investigating Megaspeed over "suspected breaches of our domestic laws" after a US senator requested the Commerce Department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips. Last month, the home affairs ministry responded to remarks in the Wall Street Journal that Singapore was concerned about Alice Huang's ties to Jensen Huang, with authorities separately investigating her alleged links to Chinese intelligence. "We would like to make clear that neither the Singapore Government nor its officials said this. And there were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang," it said, while adding that investigations into Megaspeed continue. The ministry did not immediately respond to a request for further comment on Tuesday. Singapore has become a key site for Chinese firms to set up offices in recent years, in efforts to "Singapore-wash", or domicile in the trade-focused country to reduce risks from China-US tensions. Singapore has said it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries", but it acts "firmly against companies and individuals who violate our laws and are engaged in fraudulent and dishonest practices". It is currently investigating four other individuals charged with chip fraud in an unrelated case.

MUNICH, Nov 10 : The CEOs of top European chipmakers Infineon, STMicroelectronics and NXP said on Monday the region was well positioned to compete with the US and Asia in robotics and "physical AI", building on its traditional strengths in automotive and industrial technology. As AI moves from data centres into robots, vehicles and industrial machinery, demand will grow for chips and systems that can operate safely and reliably in the real world, the executives told an industry gathering in Munich, Germany. The three companies are major suppliers of the power chips, sensors and microcontrollers used in such machines, competing with US rivals including Texas Instruments and onsemi. "For me, industrial AI or physical AI is, first of all, a must win for Europe," Infineon CEO Jochen Hanebeck said. "There are so many topics where we feel that we are second to other regions."

SYDNEY, Nov 10 : Australia's internet regulator on Tuesday rejected warnings from tech giants that a proposed online safety law would trigger widespread censorship by platforms anxious to avoid liability, arguing that their business models incentivised them to maximise user engagement. The government's Digital Duty of Care legislation will force internet companies to proactively check and stop potential user harms or face fines of up to A$109 million ($75 million). Industry critics and free speech advocates say it gives regulators too much say on what content is harmful, while supporters say only a wide-ranging law can ensure an effective safety framework. The legislation has passed the House of Representatives, but needs crossbench support to clear the Senate and become law.

"I haven't seen any indication, particularly over the past two years, that companies are over-censoring," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant told a Senate inquiry, when asked about warnings the law would have a chilling effect on free speech. "Companies today are trying to show the maximum amount of material, no matter how harmful or hurtful it is to the Australian community," she said. Referring to a section of the law requiring age checks if there was a risk of a child seeing pornography,  a senior executive at Google in Australia told the hearing on Monday that the law might force the company to block under-18s from using its Gmail service.  Representatives from Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, as well as TikTok and Snap, voiced similar concerns at the hearing, saying the law could give regulators too much discretion to decide what is harmful. Inman Grant said if lawmakers considered the wording of the legislation too vague, they should include a narrower definition of harmful content. "If there is opportunity, and we can get some more specificity, this will help us from an enforcement perspective," she said.  Most cases of excessive content removal were the result of automated moderation systems operating without human oversight, rather than of regulatory pressure, she said.  The government wants the legislation, which would also give users the chance to opt out of algorithmically recommended content and see posts only from accounts they have chosen to follow, to be passed by the end of the year. TOKYO: Technology investor SoftBank Group said on Tuesday (Nov 10) it booked a net loss of 1.1 trillion yen (US$7 billion) in the July-September quarter, hit hard by hefty advance payments it made to support the buildout of data centres in the US. The result compares with 2.5 trillion yen profit in the same period a year earlier when it logged a huge investment gain on an increase in the value of its stake in ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. SoftBank's earnings are volatile and difficult to predict. Forecasts from three analysts polled by LSEG had ranged from a profit of 233 billion yen to a loss of 113 billion yen. SoftBank said it recorded a US$3.7 billion loss due to a subsidiary investing in equipment for AI data centre projects in the US with those plans later revised.

The Japanese firm's big bets on artificial intelligence - particularly the US$64.6 billion it has spent on its 13 per cent stake in OpenAI - have raised questions about how well it will be able to weather setbacks currently buffeting the sector. The Democratic Party's sweeping success in US midterm elections last week heightened expectations of regulatory scrutiny, amplifying concerns that had been growing among investors about returns for the AI industry. SoftBank's shares, like other AI stocks, have been hit hard, almost halving in value since the start of June. The sector was further rocked by the news that the FBI is looking at Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO and the face of the AI boom, after his affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. SoftBank was a major investor in the AI chipmaker in the past but no longer holds a stake. SoftBank's fortunes are increasingly tied to OpenAI and prospects for the wider AI industry as its principal investments span AI model development, data centre infrastructure, semiconductors and robotics. Nov 10 : Japanese investors became net buyers of foreign bonds for the first time in three months in October as Treasury yields eased from early-October two-and-a-half-decade highs, while selloffs in AI-linked technology stocks boosted demand for safe-haven assets. They bought a net 493.9 billion yen ($3.13 billion) of foreign bonds in their first monthly net purchase since July, Ministry of Finance data showed on Tuesday. That included 457.2 billion yen in long-term bonds — the most since May — and 36.7 billion yen in short-term bills. Japanese investors also bought a net 1.46 trillion yen of foreign stocks last month, logging their largest monthly net investment since March. The US 10-year yield, which reached 5.3645 per cent on October 7 — its highest since April 2002 — fell 36.4 basis points for the month, its sharpest monthly decline since November 2023, as concerns over the Federal Reserve's policy outlook eased and markets grew wary of the AI boom's heavy capital spending.

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 10 : The recent volatile swings in global markets are putting greater attention on the Bank of Japan's assessment of financial conditions, a key component of its policy framework that could sway the pace and timing of interest rate increases. With markets returning to some measure of calm after a steep selloff in AI stocks, many analysts expect the BOJ to keep raising interest rates, with the next hike projected to come as soon as December. But the recent rout has tested the central bank's view that brisk AI demand will underpin the economy, with the wealth effect from booming stock prices giving households and companies more spending power. It has also put the spotlight on the BOJ's financial conditions language, which serves as a key gauge of how close its policy rate is to levels deemed neutral to the economy, thus offering clues on the pace and timing of rate rises.

While the BOJ's escalating warning over inflation risks has preoccupied market participants, the less discussed guidance on financial conditions may increase in prominence if the AI market rout keeps equity prices on a downtrend, some analysts say. "The BOJ's basic view is that financial conditions remain loose, which won't immediately change just because stock prices are falling," said former BOJ official Tetsuya Inoue, who is now executive economist at Sony Financial Group. "But if asset prices remain unstable, it may hurt growth by cooling corporate mood and spending from households with stock holdings. Depending on market moves, it could give the BOJ reason to put off a rate hike in December." STOCK WEALTH EFFECT The BOJ has stressed the need to continue raising interest rates to counter upside price risks and prevent underlying inflation from overshooting its 2 per cent target. It has also justified rate hikes by saying financial conditions are loose, pointing to low real borrowing costs, strong corporate funding demand and rising bank lending. While describing interest rates and funding indicators as key measurements, the BOJ said it also looks at asset prices in gauging financial conditions since stock prices and exchange rates affect household and corporate spending. "For example, the uptrend in stock prices likely contributed to a decline in firms' cost of capital and helped support private consumption through wealth effects," the BOJ said in its quarterly outlook report released last month. Such a positive cycle might go into reverse if the stock market adjustment persists and hits Japan's once risk-averse households, who have recently piled into stocks to ride the AI boom. Japanese households' stock holdings reached 486 trillion yen ($3.08 trillion) in June, BOJ data showed, up 47 per cent from year-earlier levels, accounting for 19.3 per cent of their total wealth. "The stock wealth effect is small compared with the US, but could have a sizeable impact on consumption as many in the younger generation now hold stocks," said Seisaku Kameda, the BOJ's former top economist, who is an economist at Japan's Sompo Institute Plus. At last month's policy meeting, the BOJ said financial conditions remained accommodative "in light of recent developments in asset markets," as well as data showing still-low real rates and funding costs. But a summary of opinions from the October meeting, released on Tuesday, exposed a rift in how board members viewed the prevailing financial conditions, with some seeing little impact of past rate hikes, while others warned of the potential hit to growth. In a sign of the board's increased attention, one member called for assessing financial conditions using three measurements: the real interest rate gap, corporate finance and the bank lending channel, and asset prices. "Asset prices, in particular, are affected not only by monetary policy but other factors," as seen in rising stock prices driven by AI-related demand, the member said. For now, markets will be on the lookout for how Governor Kazuo Ueda will describe the impact of the market rout on financial conditions in a speech due on November 30, which precedes the BOJ's next policy meeting on December 17 and 18. "Theoretically, if stock prices fall, that would tighten financial conditions," a source familiar with the BOJ's thinking said, a view echoed by another source. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly. "There's still some time before the December meeting," a third source said. "Nobody knows how markets would be behaving then." ($1 = 158.0000 yen)

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 10 : The Bank of Japan estimates that its accelerated sales of exchange-traded fund (ETF) holdings will generate about 1 trillion yen ($6.33 billion) in additional annual proceeds, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Tuesday. Katayama's remarks come after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi unveiled plans last week to tap proceeds from the BOJ's ETF sales to fund investment in areas deemed vital to Japan's economic security, as the government seeks new revenue sources without relying excessively on debt issuance. The BOJ decided on October 30 to increase annual sales of its ETF holdings to 860 billion yen from 330 billion yen on a book-value basis. A portion of net profit the central bank reaps each year, including from the ETF sales, is paid to state coffers. "The BOJ has indicated additional proceeds of roughly 1 trillion yen, but the exact amount that will be remitted to the government will depend on fiscal year-end calculations and budget procedures, so we can't say precisely how much it will be," Katayama said.

FAST

LONDON, Nov 10 : Oil prices extended losses from the previous session on Tuesday after US President Donald Trump downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, easing fears of sustained Middle East supply disruptions, with prospects of oversupply also in focus. Brent crude futures were down $2.39, or 2.58 per cent at $90.18 a barrel by 0930 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell $2.11, or 2.43 per cent to $84.74.  The Brent benchmark dropped below $90 on Tuesday for the first time since August 31, having settled down 5.85 per cent in the previous session. Trump said on Monday that he plans to hold off from new military strikes against Iran after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister.

"The market continues to prioritise President Trump's more conciliatory tone toward Iran since the midterms," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. "While attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz are still occurring, they have not escalated in a way that has forced a fresh risk premium into the market."  In the physical crude oil market, the dated Brent benchmark, against which roughly two thirds of oil supply is priced, has weakened in recent weeks. The global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, some analysts said. The global surplus is estimated at around 1.4 million barrels per day in October, JPMorgan said in a report last week. On the supply side, OPEC oil output rose in October, a Reuters survey found, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports.    Brent has retreated about 23 per cent from the six-month high of $118 it touched on October 30 as fears that Trump might step up attacks on Iran after the US midterms have eased, though concerns remain over potential shipping disruption. Elsewhere, Russian and Ukrainian officials planned to meet on Tuesday for US-brokered talks — their first since February — after Trump suggested last week that a broad peace deal was possible after four and a half years of conflict.
